introduction: 🔹 What are Currency Futures? They are standardized, exchange-traded contracts to buy or sell a specific quantity of a currency pair at a future date at a price agreed upon today.
🔹 Regulators: In India, the currency derivatives market is jointly regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
👉 Cash Settlement: Unlike physical delivery in some markets, all exchange-traded currency futures in India are settled in cash (in Indian Rupees). No physical foreign currency changes hands.
key_concepts: 🔸 1. Standardized Contracts: Everything is fixed by the exchange: the underlying pair (e.g., USD-INR), the contract size, the tick size, and the expiry months. You cannot customize these.
🔸 2. Trading Cycle: Contracts are available for 12 consecutive near months. For example, in January, you can trade contracts expiring in Jan, Feb, Mar, up to next Dec.
🔸 3. Expiry Date: Contracts expire on the last working day (excluding Saturdays) of the expiry month. If the last day is a trading holiday, it expires on the previous working day.
🔸 4. Settlement Price: The final settlement at expiry happens using the RBI Reference Rate declared on the last trading day.
important_terms: 📌 Contract Size (Lot Size): The minimum amount of currency that can be traded. For USD-INR, EUR-INR, and GBP-INR, it is 1,000 units of the base currency. For JPY-INR, it is 100,000 Japanese Yen.
📌 Tick Size: The minimum price movement allowed by the exchange. For INR pairs, it is 0.25 paise (₹0.0025).
📌 Mark-to-Market (MTM): The daily calculation of profits and losses. Margin accounts are adjusted at the end of every trading day based on the closing settlement price.
📌 Open Interest (OI): The total number of outstanding active contracts that have not been settled or closed out by an offsetting trade.

📌 Initial Margin (IM) & Extreme Loss Margin (ELM): IM is calculated based on Value at Risk (VaR) to cover 99% of probable daily price changes. ELM is an additional safety cushion collected by the exchange.
exam_points: ⚠️ Crucial Numbers: Memorize the contract sizes ($1,000, €1,000, £1,000, ¥100,000) and the tick size (₹0.0025) as direct numerical questions are highly likely for this 20% weightage unit.
✅ Cross Currency Pairs: Exchanges also offer cross-currency futures like EUR-USD, GBP-USD, and USD-JPY. Their tick sizes and contract values differ slightly from INR pairs.
✅ Trading Hours: Currency derivatives markets in India typically operate from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM for INR pairs.
💡 Settlement Timing: Remember that daily MTM is settled in cash on a T+1 basis (the next working day). Final settlement upon expiry is also handled in cash.
examples: 👉 Example 1 - Tick Value Calculation: If you buy 1 lot of USD-INR ($1000). A 1-tick movement (0.0025) means a profit or loss of ₹2.50 per lot ($1000 * 0.0025).

👉 Example 2 - MTM Concept: You buy 1 lot of USD-INR at 83.0000. At the end of the day, the closing price is 83.1000. Your MTM profit is (83.1000 - 83.0000) = 0.1000. Total profit = 0.1000 * 1000 = ₹100. This ₹100 is credited to your margin account that very evening.
summary: ✅ Key Takeaway 1: Exchange-traded futures are highly standardized, tightly regulated by SEBI/RBI, and eliminate counterparty risk through the clearing corporation.
✅ Key Takeaway 2: Daily Mark-to-Market (MTM) is the backbone of the risk management system, ensuring losses do not pile up over time.

💡 Final Tip: Pay special attention to the exact contract specifications (lot sizes, tick sizes, expiry days). Understanding the mechanics of how a single trade works will help you answer scenario-based questions.
